description:
Team Behind the Horizon - Maldonado, Uruguay We are a small team from Uruguay building tools for interplanetary survival.Our project OLVIDO-1 MARSWALK is a Martian Map for Gale Crater: One Map. 6 Layers. 1 Safe Route. A 2.1 km walk with a live DFH Safety Score - Green = GO, Red = ABORT. Who we are

We love Mars, maps, and real NASA data. We work fast, we build simple things that astronauts can actually use. Skills we bring:Concept design and storytelling Mars science research with NASA open data
summary: OLVIDO-1 MARSWALK is a layered, hyperlocal map tool for a human Marswalk in Gale Crater, Mount Sharp. It combines optical, topographic, thermal, spectral, radiation and atmospheric NASA data into one astronaut HUD view to plan a safe 2.1 km route to study boxwork formations. The route is evaluated in real-time by a DFH trend-detection algorithm and supported by the conceptual g55-MK2.1 photonic propulsion system for rapid safe extraction. The astronaut opens OLVIDO-1 MARSWALK on a tablet/HUD. The tool shows a 2.1 km route with 3 science stops. Each layer can be toggled. DFH algorithm calculates a Safety Score from slope >25°, radiation, thermal variation and dust. If score drops, route is re-calculated. The g55-MK2.1 is presented as a theoretical propulsion concept (DFH v1.4) for future Mars logistics, with a validation roadmap MK0.1 (10kW, 1mm bubble, atomic clock test). Tools: Python, Leaflet, NASA open data

PROJECT DETAILS - OLVIDO-1 MARSWALK What does it do? How does it work?

OLVIDO-1 MARSWALK is a Martian Map for Gale Crater, Mount Sharp. One Map. 6 Layers. 1 Safe Route.It guides an astronaut on a 2.1 km walk with 3 science stops:Boxwork - ancient water structures Clays - minerals that could have held life Overlook - safe view of Mount Sharp The user turns layers on and off: Optical, Topographic, Thermal, Spectral, Radiation, Atmospheric.Our DFH Safety Score combines Slope + Radiation + Temperature + Wind into one simple decision:

80-100 = Green, SAFE - GO

50-79 = Yellow, CAUTION

0-49 = Red, DANGER - ABORTExample: Radiation 0.8 mSv/hr, Slope 6 degrees, Temperature -18°C, Wind 4 m/s = Score 92, SAFE - GO.What benefits does it have?

Today NASA data is scattered. An astronaut has to check 6 different tools to know if a walk is safe. We put it all in one map. No science degree needed to understand GO or ABORT. It saves time, reduces risk, and makes science stops more valuable because the route is pre-planned for safety and science.What is the intended impact?

Walk Safe. Explore More. If astronauts can walk safely, they can explore more, collect better samples, and stay alive. Our concept scales from Gale Crater to Jezero Crater, to the Moon, and to future interplanetary missions. It is a survival guide, not just a map.What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?NASA Open Data: HiRISE, CTX, MOLA, THEMIS, CRISM, RAD (Curiosity), MEDA (Perseverance)NASA Tools: NASA PDS, JMARS, NASA Eyes on the Solar System Design: Google Slides, Canva for presentation Concept Prototyping: Google Drive, AI-assisted concept art for visualization DFH Safety Score logic: Manual prototype based on real mission thresholds for slope, radiation, temperature, and wind How is your project creative?

We turned 6 complex NASA datasets into one human decision: GO or ABORT. We added a story: OLVIDO-1, a future mission with a theoretical propulsion concept g55-MK2.1 - Dodecahedral Resonator, 50m Shield Bubble. That future vision is clearly separated from the real map. It shows where we want to go, while the map shows what we can do today.What factors did your team consider?

Safety first. Slope for walking and rover traffic, radiation exposure for human health, thermal extremes for suit and equipment, wind for dust and visibility, mineral science value for sample collection, and simplicity for use in a spacesuit with limited time and visibility.Team Behind the Horizon - Punta del Este, Uruguay.
